narrative:
The 2018 Kansas City Royals were a team in transition, still carrying the roster bones of a 2015 World Series champion but stripped of the depth and fortune that had made that run possible. They stumbled out of the gate in March and never truly recovered, losing 19 of their first 26 games in April as the bullpen — Brandon Maurer in particular — became a revolving door of late-game disasters. The franchise that had dazzled baseball with its lockdown relief corps just three years prior now watched opponents celebrate at Kauffman Stadium with alarming regularity.

May offered a brief, tantalizing reprieve. The Royals went 13-15, a near-.500 record that felt like a lifeline. Moments like Alcides Escobar's go-ahead home run on May 29th and Jorge Soler's clutch three-run shot kept hope flickering, even as Kelvin Herrera — a cornerstone of those championship bullpens — was clearly running out of gas before his inevitable trade. June erased any optimism almost entirely, as the team collapsed to 5-21 in the season's worst month, punctuated by a grand slam surrendered to Evan Gattis that epitomized the pitching staff's inability to protect leads.

The second half brought the emergence of the next generation. Ryan O'Hearn and Hunter Dozier began showing flashes of the power the franchise hoped would anchor its rebuild, and Whit Merrifield — already one of baseball's most underrated players — delivered the season's single most impactful moment on September 1st, a walk-off home run that sent Kauffman into a frenzy. Drew Butera's unlikely inside-the-park home run in July captured the scrappy, anything-for-a-win spirit that kept this diminished roster competitive on certain nights.

The Royals finished 58-104, their worst record since 1970, and the numbers told the whole story: a 4.94 ERA, a .697 OPS, and 195 more runs allowed than scored. Yet buried inside that wreckage were the seeds of tomorrow — Mondesi's speed, O'Hearn's pop, Merrifield's consistency. The 2018 season was painful to live through, but it served its purpose as the price of a rebuild, clearing the decks for a younger, hungrier Royals team to one day chase October again.

chapters.title: Opening Wounds
chapters.description: A brutal April sets the tone as the bullpen hemorrhages runs and Kansas City sinks to one of the worst records in baseball.

chapters.title: Brief Flicker
chapters.description: May brings a near-.500 record and isolated moments of brilliance, offering a deceptive glimpse of what this roster could still do.

chapters.title: June Collapse
chapters.description: The Royals go 5-21 in their worst month of the year, with the pitching staff unable to contain anyone as the season effectively ends.

chapters.title: Unlikely Heroes
chapters.description: July and early August produce improbable highlights — an inside-the-park homer, a Merrifield three-run blast — as the young core begins to show itself.

chapters.title: September Glimmer
chapters.description: A 15-13 finish gives the rebuild a hopeful final note, with Merrifield's walk-off home run standing as the season's most electric moment.
